cobalt_kable <- function(x, caption = NULL, digits = 4) {
  is_knitting <- !is.null(knitr::opts_knit$get("rmarkdown.pandoc.to"))
  if (!is_knitting) {
    knitr::kable(
      x, digits = digits, caption = caption,
      format = "html",
      table.attr = 'style="color:#FFFFFF !important; background-color:transparent !important;"'
    )
  } else if (knitr::is_html_output()) {
    knitr::kable(
      x, digits = digits, caption = caption,
      format = "html",
      table.attr = 'style="color:#222222 !important; background-color:transparent !important;"'
    )
  } else {
    knitr::kable(
      x, digits = digits, caption = caption,
      format = "latex",
      booktabs = FALSE
    )
  }
}

# Download one month early: the January 2018 log change needs December 2017 as its base
download_from <- as.Date("2017-12-01")
download_to   <- as.Date("2025-12-31")

sample_end   <- as.Date("2025-12-01")

# Section 4 — The Candidate Regressors and Their Required Transformations

This table reproduces the case brief. The **Source route** column determines whether a series is downloaded automatically or imported from the local file.

```{r variable-dictionary}
variable_dictionary <- tribble(
  ~`#`, ~Candidate_Regressor,                 ~Dataset_Code,                  ~Transformation,           ~Source,                        ~Route,
  0,    "BDO monthly log return (DEPENDENT)", "BDO_Return",                   "Monthly log return",      "Local CSV (price history)",    "Local CSV",
  1,    "PSEi return",                        "PSEi_Return",                  "Monthly log return",      "Local CSV (price history)",    "Local CSV",
  2,    "BSP RRP rate change",                "BSP_RRP_Change",               "Month-end first difference", "BSP",                         "Local CSV",
  3,    "PH 10Y gov't-yield change",          "PH_10Y_Change",                "Month-end first difference", "Instructor-supplied",         "Local CSV",
  4,    "USD/PHP change",                     "USD_PHP_Change",               "Monthly log change",      "BSP monthly FX / Yahoo (PHP=X)", "Download",
  5,    "CPI inflation",                      "PH_CPI_YoY",                   "YoY % change",            "PSA OpenSTAT",                 "Local CSV",
  6,    "M3 growth",                          "PH_M3_YoY",                    "YoY % growth",            "BSP Domestic Liquidity",       "Omitted (no data)",
  7,    "OFW remittance growth",              "PH_OFW_Remittances_YoY",       "YoY % growth",            "BSP OF remittances",           "Local CSV",
  8,    "Manufacturing-production growth",    "PH_Manufacturing_Production_YoY", "YoY % growth",         "PSA MISSI",                    "Local CSV",
  9,    "WTI return",                         "WTI_Return",                   "Monthly log return",      "FRED DCOILWTICO",              "Download",
  10,   "VIX",                                "VIX",                          "Monthly average",         "FRED VIXCLS",                  "Download"
)

variable_dictionary |>
  research_flextable()
```

**Units to keep in mind before interpreting any coefficient later:**

- Returns and log changes (`BDO_Return`, `PSEi_Return`, `USD_PHP_Change`, `WTI_Return`) are in **decimals** (0.01 = 1%).
  The local CSV stores `BDO_return` and `PSEI_return` in **percent**, so they are divided by 100 on import to match.
- Rate and yield changes (`BSP_RRP_Change`, `PH_10Y_Change`) are in **percentage points**.
- Year-over-year variables (`*_YoY`) are in **percent** (5 = 5%).
- `VIX` is an **index level**.
- `USD_PHP_Change > 0` means the **peso depreciated** (more PHP per USD).

# Section 5 — Download USD/PHP from Yahoo Finance

BDO and the PSEi now come from the local CSV (Section 9). Only USD/PHP is still downloaded from Yahoo Finance. The helper below returns `NULL` (instead of crashing the whole document) if a download fails, so the problem is easy to diagnose.

```{r yahoo-download}
safe_get <- function(symbol, src) {
  tryCatch(
    suppressWarnings(
      getSymbols(symbol, src = src,
                 from = download_from, to = download_to,
                 auto.assign = FALSE)
    ),
    error = function(e) {
      message("Download failed for ", symbol, " (", src, "): ", conditionMessage(e))
      NULL
    }
  )
}

# Use the adjusted close when it exists (equities); otherwise the close (index, FX).
price_series <- function(x) {
  if (is.null(x)) return(NULL)
  if (has.Ad(x)) Ad(x) else Cl(x)
}

usdphp_raw <- safe_get("PHP=X", "yahoo")   # USD/PHP exchange rate (PHP per USD)
usdphp_px  <- price_series(usdphp_raw)
```

# Section 6 — Download Global Variables from FRED

```{r fred-download}
vix_raw <- safe_get("VIXCLS",      "FRED")   # CBOE VIX, daily close
wti_raw <- safe_get("DCOILWTICO",  "FRED")   # WTI crude oil, daily spot
```

# Section 7 — Inspect Frequencies and Timing

The series do not arrive at the same frequency or on the same dates. Aligning them correctly is part of the research design.

```{r frequency-inspection}
tibble(
  Series = c("PHP=X", "VIXCLS", "DCOILWTICO",
             "BDO", "PSEi", "BSP RRP rate", "PH 10Y yield", "PH CPI",
             "OFW remittances", "Manufacturing production"),
  Source = c(rep("Download", 3), rep("Local CSV", 7)),
  Monthly_Rule = c("Monthly average", "Monthly average", "Monthly average",
                   "Already monthly (log return)", "Already monthly (log return)",
                   "Already monthly (first difference)", "Already monthly (first difference)",
                   "Already monthly (YoY %)", "Already monthly (YoY %)",
                   "Already monthly (YoY %)")
) |>
  cobalt_kable(caption = "Source and Monthly Aggregation Rule")
```

**Why these rules?**

- USD/PHP: BSP publishes **monthly average** exchange rates, so the monthly average of daily quotes is the closest match.
- VIX and WTI: **monthly average**, as specified in the brief.
- BDO, PSEi, the policy rate and yield, CPI, remittances and manufacturing arrive in the local CSV already as monthly returns, first differences or YoY rates.
- M3 growth is omitted because no usable data could be found online.

# Section 8 — Convert the Downloaded Series to a Common Monthly Key

Every series is converted to a `yearmon` key (e.g., "Jan 2018") **before** joining. This avoids silently losing observations because one source stamps a month on its first day and another on its last.

```{r monthly-helpers}
monthly_df_xts <- function(x, name, how = c("last", "mean")) {
  how <- match.arg(how)
  if (is.null(x)) return(NULL)

  tibble(
    date  = as.Date(index(x)),
    value = as.numeric(x[, 1])
  ) |>
    filter(is.finite(value)) |>
    arrange(date) |>
    mutate(month = as.yearmon(date)) |>
    group_by(month) |>
    summarise(
      value = if (how == "last") dplyr::last(value) else mean(value),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    rename(!!name := value)
}

# --- Daily market series -> monthly averages ---
usdphp_df <- monthly_df_xts(usdphp_px, "USD_PHP", how = "mean")
vix_df    <- monthly_df_xts(vix_raw,   "VIX",     how = "mean")
wti_df    <- monthly_df_xts(wti_raw,   "WTI",     how = "mean")
```

```{r preview-monthly}
# View the first few rows of the monthly aggregated data
head(usdphp_df)
head(vix_df)
head(wti_df)
```
# Section 9 — Load the Local CSV (BDO, PSEi, BSP / PSA Series)

The local CSV already contains the transformed series (BDO and PSEi returns, month-end first differences, YoY rates), so **no further transformation is applied**. It is used exactly as supplied; the only step is turning the `month` label into a `yearmon` key so it can be joined to the downloaded data.

**M3 growth is omitted** from this dataset because no usable data could be found online.

```{r load-local}
if (!file.exists(local_file)) {
  stop("Cannot find '", local_file, "'. Place it in the same folder as this .Rmd.")
}

local_df <- readr::read_csv(local_file, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(month = as.yearmon(month, format = "%b %Y"))

stopifnot(!anyNA(local_df$month), !anyDuplicated(local_df$month))

head(local_df)
```

# Section 10 — Log Changes for the Downloaded Series

Only the downloaded data needs transforming. USD/PHP and WTI use `log(level_t) - log(level_{t-1})`; VIX stays as a monthly average level. December 2017 is in the downloaded data only to supply the base for January 2018 and is dropped by the join.

```{r market-transforms}
market_list <- list(USD_PHP = usdphp_df, VIX = vix_df, WTI = wti_df)

failed <- names(Filter(is.null, market_list))
if (length(failed) > 0) {
  stop("These downloads failed, so the dataset cannot be built: ",
       paste(failed, collapse = ", "))
}

log_change <- function(x) log(x) - dplyr::lag(log(x))

market_df <- usdphp_df |>
  full_join(vix_df, by = "month") |>
  full_join(wti_df, by = "month") |>
  arrange(month) |>
  mutate(
    USD_PHP_Change = log_change(USD_PHP),
    WTI_Return     = log_change(WTI)
  ) |>
  select(month, USD_PHP_Change, WTI_Return, VIX)

head(market_df)
```


# Section 11 — Join the Downloaded Data with the CSV Data

A complete monthly spine (Jan 2018 to Dec 2025) is built first, and each table is left-joined to it on the `yearmon` key. Any month missing from a source therefore shows up as an `NA` instead of silently disappearing.

```{r join-tables}
month_spine <- tibble(
  month = as.yearmon(seq(sample_start, sample_end, by = "month"))
)

analysis_df <- month_spine |>
  left_join(local_df,  by = "month") |>
  left_join(market_df, by = "month")

analysis_df |>
  head(12) |>
  cobalt_kable(caption = "Analysis Dataset (first 12 months)")
```

```{r join-checks}
tibble(
  Check = c("Rows (expected 96)", "Columns (month + dependent + regressors)",
            "First month", "Last month", "Total missing values"),
  Result = c(nrow(analysis_df), ncol(analysis_df),
             format(min(analysis_df$month)), format(max(analysis_df$month)),
             sum(is.na(analysis_df)))
) |>
  cobalt_kable(caption = "Join Checks")

# Missing values per column (all should be 0)
analysis_df |>
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Missing") |>
  cobalt_kable(caption = "Missing Values by Variable")

# Save the ready-to-model table
readr::write_csv(
  analysis_df |> mutate(month = format(month)),
  "analysis_dataset.csv"
)
view(analysis_df)
```

# Section 12 — Baseline Multiple Linear Regression

A single baseline model using every available column as a regressor (M3 excluded), fitted on the full sample. Only its fit is reported here.

```{r baseline-lm}
dep_var <- "BDO_return"   # dependent variable: BDO monthly log return (column name in the local CSV)

model_data <- analysis_df |>
  select(-month) |>
  drop_na()

baseline_lm <- lm(reformulate(".", response = dep_var), data = model_data)

# --- Regression accuracy (in-sample) ---
tibble(
  Metric = c("Observations used", "R-squared", "Adjusted R-squared", "RMSE", "MAE"),
  Value  = c(nobs(baseline_lm),
             summary(baseline_lm)$r.squared,
             summary(baseline_lm)$adj.r.squared,
             sqrt(mean(residuals(baseline_lm)^2)),
             mean(abs(residuals(baseline_lm))))
) |>
  cobalt_kable(caption = "Baseline Linear Regression — Fit (in-sample)")
coef(baseline_lm)
```





# 4.3 Statistical Inference

The baseline model is used to check how each factor is related to BDO's monthly return while accounting for the other factors. Changes in BDO return are measured in percentage points. These results describe associations and do not establish cause and effect.


## 4.3.1 Individual Coefficient Tests

Each factor is tested at the 5% significance level. The test allows for either a positive or negative relationship, so it is called a two-sided test.

- **Null hypothesis (H0):** The factor's coefficient is zero. It has no linear association with BDO return once the other factors in the model are taken into account.
- **Alternative hypothesis (H1):** The factor's coefficient is not zero. It has a positive or negative linear association with BDO return once the other factors are taken into account.

A factor's coefficient shows the estimated change in BDO return for a one-unit increase in that factor, holding the other included variables constant.

- **Zero coefficient:** No linear association with BDO return within this model.
- **Positive coefficient:** A higher factor value is associated with higher BDO return.
- **Negative coefficient:** A higher factor value is associated with lower BDO return.

An estimate can be positive or negative even when the evidence is too weak to call it statistically significant.

```{r inference-individual-hypotheses}
# Set up the hypotheses for the constant and the nine factors
individual_hypotheses <- tibble(
  Term = names(coef(baseline_lm)),
  H0 = "This coefficient equals zero",
  H1 = "This coefficient differs from zero"
)

individual_hypotheses |>
  mutate(
    Term = if_else(
      Term == "(Intercept)",
      "Constant (intercept)",
      Term
    )
  ) |>
  flextable::flextable()
```


```{r inference-coefficient-tests}
# Keep the full values when making decisions and calculating effects
inference_alpha <- 0.05

factor_details <- tribble(
  ~term, ~Variable, ~Scenario, ~Scenario_Change,

  "PSEI_return",
  "PSEi return",
  "+1 percentage point in market return",
  1,

  "BSP_RRP",
  "BSP policy-rate change",
  "+0.25 percentage points in rate change",
  0.25,

  "PH_10Y_Yield",
  "PH 10Y yield change",
  "+0.25 percentage points in yield change",
  0.25,

  "CPI",
  "CPI inflation",
  "+1 percentage point in YoY inflation",
  1,

  "OFW_remittance",
  "OFW remittance growth",
  "+5 percentage points in YoY growth",
  5,

  "manafactuting_prod_growth",
  "Manufacturing growth",
  "+10 percentage points in YoY growth",
  10,

  "USD_PHP_Change",
  "USD/PHP log change",
  "+1% in the exchange-rate ratio (peso depreciation)",
  log(1.01),

  "WTI_Return",
  "WTI log return",
  "+10% in the oil-price ratio",
  log(1.10),

  "VIX",
  "VIX",
  "+10 index points",
  10
)

# Use the column names exactly as they appear in the CSV
stopifnot(setequal(
  factor_details$term,
  setdiff(names(coef(baseline_lm)), "(Intercept)")
))

coefficient_results <- broom::tidy(
  baseline_lm,
  conf.int = TRUE,
  conf.level = 1 - inference_alpha
) |>
  left_join(
    factor_details |> select(term, Variable),
    by = "term"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Variable = coalesce(Variable, "Constant (intercept)"),
    Decision = case_when(
      term == "(Intercept)" & p.value < inference_alpha ~
        "Reject H0; evidence that the intercept differs from zero",

      term == "(Intercept)" ~
        "Fail to reject H0; insufficient evidence that the intercept differs from zero",

      p.value < inference_alpha ~
        "Reject H0; evidence of a linear association with BDO return",

      TRUE ~
        "Fail to reject H0; insufficient evidence of a linear association with BDO return"
    )
  )

coefficient_results |>
  select(
    Variable,
    estimate,
    std.error,
    statistic,
    p.value,
    Decision
  ) |>
  mutate(
    p.value = format.pval(
      p.value,
      digits = 3,
      eps = 0.0001
    )
  ) |>
  flextable::flextable()
```


## 4.3.2 Confidence Intervals and Parameter Uncertainty

The 95% confidence interval shows a range of values consistent with the coefficient estimate and its uncertainty. A wider interval means the estimate is less precise. If the interval includes zero, there is not enough evidence to say that the coefficient differs from zero at the 5% significance level.

```{r inference-confidence-intervals}
# Find the 95% confidence interval for each coefficient
confidence_intervals <- confint(
  baseline_lm,
  level = 1 - inference_alpha
) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("term")

names(confidence_intervals) <- c(
  "term",
  "Lower_95",
  "Upper_95"
)

confidence_intervals <- confidence_intervals |>
  left_join(
    coefficient_results |>
      select(term, Variable, estimate),
    by = "term"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Includes_Zero = if_else(
      Lower_95 <= 0 & Upper_95 >= 0,
      "Yes",
      "No"
    )
  )

confidence_intervals |>
  select(
    Variable,
    estimate,
    Lower_95,
    Upper_95,
    Includes_Zero
  ) |>
  flextable::flextable()
```


## 4.3.3 Statistical versus Economic Significance

Statistical significance tells us whether there is enough evidence to detect a relationship. Economic significance asks whether the estimated change in BDO return is large enough to matter financially. The tables below show estimated changes for a typical movement in each factor and for selected scenarios.

```{r inference-economic-significance}
# Use each factor's units when working out the estimated changes
bdo_return_sd <- sd(model_data[[dep_var]])

economic_effects <- coefficient_results |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  left_join(
    factor_details |> select(-Variable),
    by = "term"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Factor_SD = vapply(
      term,
      function(variable) sd(model_data[[variable]]),
      numeric(1)
    ),

    One_SD_Effect = estimate * Factor_SD,

    Significant_at_5pct = if_else(
      p.value < inference_alpha,
      "Yes",
      "No"
    ),

    Effect_as_Pct_of_BDO_SD =
      100 * abs(One_SD_Effect) / bdo_return_sd,

    Scenario_Effect = estimate * Scenario_Change,
    Scenario_Lower_95 = conf.low * Scenario_Change,
    Scenario_Upper_95 = conf.high * Scenario_Change
  )

economic_effects |>
  select(
    Variable,
    Significant_at_5pct,
    One_SD_Effect,
    Effect_as_Pct_of_BDO_SD
  ) |>
  flextable::flextable()

economic_effects |>
  select(
    Variable,
    Scenario,
    Scenario_Effect,
    Scenario_Lower_95,
    Scenario_Upper_95
  ) |>
  flextable::flextable()
```

One standard deviation (One-SD) describes how much a factor typically varies in this sample. The percentage column compares the size of the estimated change with BDO's usual monthly variation. It is not the share of returns explained by the model. The scenario intervals show uncertainty around the estimated changes; they are not forecasts of future returns.


## 4.3.4 Joint Hypothesis Tests

The first test asks whether the nine factors together help explain BDO returns. The second asks whether the other eight factors add information beyond PSEi alone. Each group is tested as a whole, so a significant result does not tell us which individual factors matter.

```{r inference-joint-hypotheses}
joint_hypotheses <- tribble(
  ~Test, ~H0, ~H1,

  "Overall contribution of all factors",
  "All nine slope coefficients equal zero",
  "At least one of the nine slope coefficients differs from zero",

  "Additional contribution beyond PSEi",
  "All eight non-PSEi slope coefficients equal zero",
  "At least one of the eight non-PSEi slope coefficients differs from zero"
)

joint_hypotheses |>
  flextable::flextable()
```

```{r inference-joint-tests}
# Fit the PSEi-only model using the same months as the baseline
market_lm <- lm(
  BDO_return ~ PSEI_return,
  data = model_data
)

# Test whether the eight other factors add information beyond PSEi
nonmarket_joint_test <- anova(
  market_lm,
  baseline_lm
)

# Get the overall F-test from the baseline model
overall_f <- summary(baseline_lm)$fstatistic

joint_test_results <- tibble(
  Test = joint_hypotheses$Test,

  F_Statistic = c(
    unname(overall_f[1]),
    nonmarket_joint_test[["F"]][2]
  ),

  Numerator_DF = c(
    unname(overall_f[2]),
    nonmarket_joint_test[["Df"]][2]
  ),

  Denominator_DF = c(
    unname(overall_f[3]),
    nonmarket_joint_test[["Res.Df"]][2]
  ),

  p.value = c(
    pf(
      overall_f[1],
      overall_f[2],
      overall_f[3],
      lower.tail = FALSE
    ),
    nonmarket_joint_test[["Pr(>F)"]][2]
  )
) |>
  mutate(
    Decision = if_else(
      p.value < inference_alpha,
      "Reject H0; evidence that the tested group contributes explanatory information",
      "Fail to reject H0; insufficient evidence that the tested group contributes explanatory information"
    )
  )

joint_test_results |>
  mutate(
    p.value = format.pval(
      p.value,
      digits = 3,
      eps = 0.0001
    )
  ) |>
  flextable::flextable()
```

These tests assume that the unexplained part of BDO returns has a similar spread throughout the sample and is not correlated across months. If either assumption is wrong, the p-values and confidence intervals may not reflect the true level of uncertainty.















# 4.4 Model Evaluation and Comparison

Compare three models to see whether adding more factors improves how well they explain BDO returns. Each model uses the same months and the same measure of BDO return to compare them fairly.


## 4.4.1 Models Being Compared

- **Market benchmark:** Uses PSEi returns to represent movements in the Philippine stock market.
- **Market + domestic conditions:** Starts with PSEi and adds changes in the policy rate, government yield, and exchange rate, plus inflation, remittance growth, and manufacturing growth.
- **Full baseline:** Adds WTI returns and VIX to the domestic model to account for energy prices and global uncertainty.

M3 growth is not available in our dataset, so these models do not directly measure domestic liquidity.

```{r comparison-models}
# Reuse the market model and the full baseline
domestic_lm <- lm(
  BDO_return ~ PSEI_return + BSP_RRP + PH_10Y_Yield + USD_PHP_Change + 
    CPI + OFW_remittance + manafactuting_prod_growth,
  data = model_data
)

comparison_models <- list(
  "Market benchmark" = market_lm,
  "Market + domestic conditions" = domestic_lm,
  "Full baseline" = baseline_lm
)

# Check that each model uses the same months and BDO returns
baseline_frame <- model.frame(baseline_lm)

stopifnot(all(vapply(
  comparison_models,
  function(fit) {
    identical(
      rownames(model.frame(fit)),
      rownames(baseline_frame)
    ) &&
      identical(
        model.response(model.frame(fit)),
        model.response(baseline_frame)
      )
  },
  logical(1)
)))
```


## 4.4.2 Model Fit and Complexity

- **N / Slopes:** Number of months / explanatory factors, excluding the constant.
- **R-squared:** Share of variation in BDO returns explained by the model. A higher value means a closer fit in this sample.
- **Adjusted R-squared:** Adjusts for the number of factors, so adding factors does not always raise it.
- **AIC/BIC:** Compare fit while accounting for extra parameters. Lower values are preferred when models use the same outcome and observations.

```{r comparison-fit-table}
# Keep the full values when comparing the models
model_comparison <- purrr::imap_dfr(
  comparison_models,
  function(fit, model_name) {
    tibble(
      Model = model_name,
      N = nobs(fit),
      Slopes = length(coef(fit)) - 1,
      R_Squared = summary(fit)$r.squared,
      Adjusted_R_Squared = summary(fit)$adj.r.squared,
      AIC = AIC(fit),
      BIC = BIC(fit),
      RMSE = sqrt(mean(residuals(fit)^2)),
      MAE = mean(abs(residuals(fit)))
    )
  }
)

model_comparison |>
  select(
    Model,
    N,
    Slopes,
    R_Squared,
    Adjusted_R_Squared,
    AIC,
    BIC
  ) |>
  flextable::flextable()
```

- **RMSE:** Summarizes the gaps between actual and fitted BDO returns. Large gaps have more weight in this measure.
- **MAE:** Shows the average size of those gaps, whether the model estimates returns too high or too low.

Both measures are in percentage points. Lower values mean the fitted returns are closer to the actual returns in this sample. A separate check would be needed using new observations to assess future predictions.

```{r comparison-errors}
model_comparison |>
  select(Model, RMSE, MAE) |>
  flextable::flextable()
```


## 4.4.3 Nested-Model Comparisons

Each test compares a smaller model with one that contains all its factors plus some extra ones. The first adds six domestic factors to the PSEi model. The second adds WTI returns and VIX to the domestic model. Each test checks whether the added group helps explain BDO returns.

- **Null hypothesis (H0):** The added factors' coefficients are all zero. They have no additional linear association with BDO return after accounting for the factors already in the model.
- **Alternative hypothesis (H1):** At least one added coefficient is not zero. At least one added factor has an additional linear association with BDO return.

```{r comparison-nested-hypotheses}
nested_hypotheses <- tribble(
  ~Comparison, ~H0, ~H1,

  "Domestic conditions beyond market",
  "All six added domestic coefficients equal zero",
  "At least one of the six added domestic coefficients differs from zero",

  "Global factors beyond domestic model",
  "The WTI and VIX coefficients both equal zero",
  "At least one of the WTI and VIX coefficients differs from zero"
)

nested_hypotheses |>
  flextable::flextable()
```

`Added_Slopes` is the number of added factors. `RSS_Reduction` is the drop in total squared fitting errors. The F-statistic compares that improvement with the error remaining in the larger model. If the p-value is below 0.05, reject H0. Otherwise, there is not enough evidence that the added group improves the model.

```{r comparison-nested-tests}
# Compare each smaller model with the model containing the added factors
nested_tests <- list(
  "Domestic conditions beyond market" =
    anova(market_lm, domestic_lm),

  "Global factors beyond domestic model" =
    anova(domestic_lm, baseline_lm)
)

nested_test_results <- purrr::imap_dfr(
  nested_tests,
  function(test, test_name) {
    tibble(
      Comparison = test_name,
      Added_Slopes = test[["Df"]][2],
      RSS_Reduction = test[["Sum of Sq"]][2],
      F_Statistic = test[["F"]][2],
      Denominator_DF = test[["Res.Df"]][2],
      p.value = test[["Pr(>F)"]][2]
    )
  }
) |>
  mutate(
    Decision = if_else(
      p.value < inference_alpha,
      "Reject H0; evidence that the added factors improve explanatory fit",
      "Fail to reject H0; insufficient evidence that the added factors improve explanatory fit"
    )
  )

nested_test_results |>
  mutate(
    p.value = format.pval(
      p.value,
      digits = 3,
      eps = 0.0001
    )
  ) |>
  flextable::flextable()
```


## 4.4.4 PSEi Coefficient across Models

For each model, the estimate shows the expected change in BDO return for a one-percentage-point increase in PSEi return, holding the other included factors constant. The estimated change is also in percentage points. The confidence limits show how uncertain the estimate is. The rows are compared to see how the PSEi estimate changes as factors are added; this is not a formal test of equal coefficients.

```{r comparison-market-coefficient}
# Compare the PSEi estimate and its confidence interval across the models
market_coefficient_comparison <- purrr::imap_dfr(
  comparison_models,
  function(fit, model_name) {
    broom::tidy(
      fit,
      conf.int = TRUE,
      conf.level = 1 - inference_alpha
    ) |>
      filter(term == "PSEI_return") |>
      mutate(Model = model_name)
  }
)

market_coefficient_comparison |>
  select(
    Model,
    estimate,
    conf.low,
    conf.high,
    p.value
  ) |>
  mutate(
    p.value = format.pval(
      p.value,
      digits = 3,
      eps = 0.0001
    )
  ) |>
  flextable::flextable()
```


## 4.4.5 Comparison Summary

This table shows which model scores best on each measure. A higher adjusted R-squared and lower AIC and BIC are looked for. These results help us compare models, but the final choice should also consider financial reasoning, uncertainty, and the tests of added factors. A model should not be chosen just because it has the largest R-squared.

```{r comparison-summary}
best_adjusted_r2_model <- model_comparison$Model[
  which.max(model_comparison$Adjusted_R_Squared)
]

lowest_aic_model <- model_comparison$Model[
  which.min(model_comparison$AIC)
]

lowest_bic_model <- model_comparison$Model[
  which.min(model_comparison$BIC)
]

criterion_summary <- tibble(
  Criterion = c(
    "Highest adjusted R-squared",
    "Lowest AIC",
    "Lowest BIC"
  ),
  Model = c(
    best_adjusted_r2_model,
    lowest_aic_model,
    lowest_bic_model
  )
)

criterion_summary |>
  flextable::flextable()
```






# 4.5 Regression Diagnostics

The tests in 4.3 and 4.4 rely on assumptions about the baseline model's errors (the part of BDO's return the model does not explain). This section checks those assumptions one at a time. Each check uses the full baseline model (`baseline_lm`) and the same 5% significance level as 4.3 (`inference_alpha`).

```{r diag-setup}
# Shared objects for the diagnostics
diag_resid  <- residuals(baseline_lm)
diag_fitted <- fitted(baseline_lm)
diag_n      <- nobs(baseline_lm)
diag_k      <- length(coef(baseline_lm)) - 1   # number of slopes (excludes the constant)

# Month labels for the observations actually used in the model
diag_months <- analysis_df |>
  drop_na() |>
  pull(month)

stopifnot(length(diag_months) == diag_n)

regressor_names <- setdiff(names(coef(baseline_lm)), "(Intercept)")
```


## 4.5.1 Multicollinearity

Multicollinearity happens when two or more factors move closely together, so the model cannot separate their individual effects. It does not bias the estimates, but it widens their standard errors.

- **Correlation matrix:** Pairwise correlations between factors. Values close to +1 or -1 are a warning sign.
- **Variance Inflation Factor (VIF):** How much a coefficient's variance is inflated because that factor can be predicted from the other factors. VIF = 1 / (1 - R²), where R² comes from regressing that factor on all the other factors. A VIF above 5 is a concern and above 10 is serious.

```{r diag-correlation}
# Pairwise correlations between the regressors only
regressor_correlations <- model_data |>
  select(all_of(regressor_names)) |>
  cor()

regressor_correlations |>
  round(2) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("Variable") |>
  flextable::flextable()

# Largest absolute pairwise correlation
correlation_pairs <- regressor_correlations |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("Variable_1") |>
  pivot_longer(-Variable_1, names_to = "Variable_2", values_to = "Correlation") |>
  filter(Variable_1 < Variable_2) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(Correlation)))

correlation_pairs |>
  head(5) |>
  flextable::flextable()
```

```{r diag-correlation-heatmap, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6}
regressor_correlations |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("Variable_1") |>
  pivot_longer(-Variable_1, names_to = "Variable_2", values_to = "Correlation") |>
  ggplot(aes(Variable_1, Variable_2, fill = Correlation)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(Correlation, 2)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "grey30", mid = "white", high = "grey30",
                       midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Correlation between regressors", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

```{r diag-vif}
# VIF computed directly: regress each factor on all the other factors
vif_results <- tibble(term = regressor_names) |>
  mutate(
    Auxiliary_R2 = vapply(
      term,
      function(variable) {
        others <- setdiff(regressor_names, variable)
        summary(lm(reformulate(others, response = variable), data = model_data))$r.squared
      },
      numeric(1)
    ),
    VIF = 1 / (1 - Auxiliary_R2),
    Assessment = case_when(
      VIF > 10 ~ "Serious multicollinearity",
      VIF > 5  ~ "Moderate concern",
      TRUE     ~ "No concern"
    )
  )

vif_results |>
  flextable::flextable()
```


## 4.5.2 Heteroskedasticity

Heteroskedasticity means the spread of the errors changes across observations, for example larger errors in volatile months. The coefficients stay unbiased, but the usual standard errors, and so the p-values and confidence intervals in 4.3, can be wrong.

- **Residuals vs. fitted plot:** If the spread of points widens or narrows as fitted values change, that suggests heteroskedasticity.
- **Breusch-Pagan test:** Regresses the squared residuals on the factors. H0: the error variance is constant (homoskedastic). H1: the error variance depends on the factors.
- **White test:** Same idea, but also includes the squared factors, so it can detect non-linear patterns in the variance.

```{r diag-resid-fitted, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5}
tibble(Fitted = diag_fitted, Residual = diag_resid) |>
  ggplot(aes(Fitted, Residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.6) +
  labs(title = "Residuals vs. fitted values",
       x = "Fitted BDO return (percentage points)",
       y = "Residual (percentage points)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r diag-heteroskedasticity}
# Breusch-Pagan: squared residuals on the original factors
bp_test <- lmtest::bptest(baseline_lm)

# White test: squared residuals on the factors and their squares
white_formula <- as.formula(paste(
  "~", paste(regressor_names, collapse = " + "), "+",
  paste0("I(", regressor_names, "^2)", collapse = " + ")
))
white_test <- lmtest::bptest(baseline_lm, white_formula, data = model_data)

heteroskedasticity_results <- tibble(
  Test = c("Breusch-Pagan", "White (with squared terms)"),
  Statistic = c(unname(bp_test$statistic), unname(white_test$statistic)),
  DF = c(unname(bp_test$parameter), unname(white_test$parameter)),
  p.value = c(bp_test$p.value, white_test$p.value)
) |>
  mutate(
    Decision = if_else(
      p.value < inference_alpha,
      "Reject H0; evidence of heteroskedasticity",
      "Fail to reject H0; no evidence of heteroskedasticity"
    )
  )

heteroskedasticity_results |>
  mutate(p.value = format.pval(p.value, digits = 3, eps = 0.0001)) |>
  flextable::flextable()
```


## 4.5.3 Autocorrelation

The data are monthly, so this month's error may be related to last month's error. If so, the usual standard errors are again unreliable.

- **Residuals over time and ACF plot:** The ACF (autocorrelation function) shows the correlation between residuals and their own past values. Bars outside the dashed bands suggest autocorrelation at that lag.
- **Durbin-Watson test:** Checks for first-order autocorrelation (this month vs. last month). A value near 2 means no autocorrelation.
- **Breusch-Godfrey test:** Checks for autocorrelation at several lags at once. Lag 1 and lag 12 (one year of monthly data) are tested. H0: no autocorrelation up to that lag. H1: some autocorrelation exists.

```{r diag-resid-time, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4}
tibble(Month = as.Date(diag_months), Residual = diag_resid) |>
  ggplot(aes(Month, Residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  labs(title = "Baseline residuals over time",
       x = NULL, y = "Residual (percentage points)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r diag-acf, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
acf(diag_resid, lag.max = 24, main = "ACF of baseline residuals")
```

```{r diag-autocorrelation}
dw_test   <- lmtest::dwtest(baseline_lm, alternative = "two.sided")
bg_test_1 <- lmtest::bgtest(baseline_lm, order = 1)
bg_test_12 <- lmtest::bgtest(baseline_lm, order = 12)

autocorrelation_results <- tibble(
  Test = c("Durbin-Watson (first order)",
           "Breusch-Godfrey (up to lag 1)",
           "Breusch-Godfrey (up to lag 12)"),
  Statistic = c(unname(dw_test$statistic),
                unname(bg_test_1$statistic),
                unname(bg_test_12$statistic)),
  p.value = c(dw_test$p.value, bg_test_1$p.value, bg_test_12$p.value)
) |>
  mutate(
    Decision = if_else(
      p.value < inference_alpha,
      "Reject H0; evidence of autocorrelation",
      "Fail to reject H0; no evidence of autocorrelation"
    )
  )

autocorrelation_results |>
  mutate(p.value = format.pval(p.value, digits = 3, eps = 0.0001)) |>
  flextable::flextable()
```


## 4.5.4 Outliers and Influential Observations

Some months may be unusual enough to pull the estimated coefficients toward them. Three measures are used:

- **Studentized residual:** How far a month's actual return is from the model's fit, in standard-error units. Values beyond 2 in absolute value are unusual; beyond 3 are outliers.
- **Leverage (hat value):** How unusual a month's factor values are compared with the rest of the sample. Values above 2(k + 1)/n are high, where k is the number of slopes and n the number of months.
- **Cook's distance:** Combines both, measuring how much all coefficients would change if that month were removed. Values above 4/n are flagged.

```{r diag-influence}
leverage_cutoff <- 2 * (diag_k + 1) / diag_n
cooks_cutoff    <- 4 / diag_n

influence_table <- tibble(
  Month = format(diag_months),
  BDO_Return = model_data[[dep_var]],
  Studentized_Residual = rstudent(baseline_lm),
  Leverage = hatvalues(baseline_lm),
  Cooks_Distance = cooks.distance(baseline_lm)
) |>
  mutate(
    Large_Residual = abs(Studentized_Residual) > 2,
    High_Leverage  = Leverage > leverage_cutoff,
    Influential    = Cooks_Distance > cooks_cutoff
  )

tibble(
  Measure = c("Studentized residual beyond 2 in absolute value",
              "Leverage above 2(k + 1)/n",
              "Cook's distance above 4/n"),
  Cutoff = c(2, leverage_cutoff, cooks_cutoff),
  Months_Flagged = c(sum(influence_table$Large_Residual),
                     sum(influence_table$High_Leverage),
                     sum(influence_table$Influential))
) |>
  flextable::flextable()

# Every month flagged by at least one measure, most influential first
flagged_months <- influence_table |>
  filter(Large_Residual | High_Leverage | Influential) |>
  arrange(desc(Cooks_Distance))

flagged_months |>
  flextable::flextable()
```

```{r diag-cooks-plot, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4}
influence_table |>
  mutate(Month = as.Date(diag_months)) |>
  ggplot(aes(Month, Cooks_Distance)) +
  geom_col(width = 20, fill = "grey40") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = cooks_cutoff, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_text(
    data = ~ filter(.x, Influential),
    aes(label = format(as.yearmon(Month))),
    vjust = -0.4, size = 3
  ) +
  labs(title = "Cook's distance by month",
       subtitle = "Dashed line: 4/n cutoff",
       x = NULL, y = "Cook's distance") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The flagged months can be linked to known events, for example the COVID-19 lockdowns in 2020 and the 2022 rate-hiking cycle. The manufacturing growth variable is checked separately, because year-over-year growth produces extreme values when the comparison month was itself abnormal (a base effect).

```{r diag-manufacturing-extremes}
# Year-over-year manufacturing growth: months with extreme readings
model_data |>
  mutate(Month = format(diag_months)) |>
  filter(abs(manafactuting_prod_growth) > 40) |>
  select(Month, manafactuting_prod_growth) |>
  flextable::flextable()
```

```{r diag-manufacturing-plot, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4}
tibble(Month = as.Date(diag_months),
       Manufacturing_YoY = model_data$manafactuting_prod_growth) |>
  ggplot(aes(Month, Manufacturing_YoY)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  labs(title = "Manufacturing production growth (YoY %)",
       x = NULL, y = "YoY growth (%)") +
  theme_minimal()
```


## 4.5.5 Residual Diagnostics

Two more checks on the residuals:

- **Normality:** The t-tests and F-tests in 4.3 assume normally distributed errors. This matters less in larger samples, but with 96 months it is still worth checking. The Q-Q plot compares the residuals with a normal distribution; points on the line mean the residuals look normal. Shapiro-Wilk and Jarque-Bera (based on skewness and kurtosis) test H0: the residuals are normally distributed.
- **Functional form (Ramsey RESET):** Checks whether adding squared and cubed fitted values improves the model. H0: the linear form is adequate. H1: the model is missing a non-linear relationship.

```{r diag-qq, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5}
tibble(Residual = diag_resid) |>
  ggplot(aes(sample = Residual)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line() +
  labs(title = "Normal Q-Q plot of baseline residuals",
       x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Sample quantiles") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r diag-residual-tests}
shapiro_result <- shapiro.test(diag_resid)

# Jarque-Bera computed directly from skewness and excess kurtosis
jb_skew <- mean((diag_resid - mean(diag_resid))^3) / mean((diag_resid - mean(diag_resid))^2)^1.5
jb_kurt <- mean((diag_resid - mean(diag_resid))^4) / mean((diag_resid - mean(diag_resid))^2)^2
jb_stat <- diag_n / 6 * (jb_skew^2 + (jb_kurt - 3)^2 / 4)
jb_p    <- pchisq(jb_stat, df = 2, lower.tail = FALSE)

reset_result <- lmtest::resettest(baseline_lm, power = 2:3, type = "fitted")

residual_test_results <- tibble(
  Test = c("Shapiro-Wilk (normality)",
           "Jarque-Bera (normality)",
           "Ramsey RESET (functional form)"),
  Statistic = c(unname(shapiro_result$statistic), jb_stat,
                unname(reset_result$statistic)),
  p.value = c(shapiro_result$p.value, jb_p, reset_result$p.value)
) |>
  mutate(
    Decision = case_when(
      str_detect(Test, "RESET") & p.value < inference_alpha ~
        "Reject H0; evidence of a missing non-linear relationship",
      str_detect(Test, "RESET") ~
        "Fail to reject H0; linear form is adequate",
      p.value < inference_alpha ~
        "Reject H0; residuals are not normal",
      TRUE ~
        "Fail to reject H0; no evidence against normality"
    )
  )

residual_test_results |>
  mutate(p.value = format.pval(p.value, digits = 3, eps = 0.0001)) |>
  flextable::flextable()

tibble(Skewness = jb_skew, Kurtosis = jb_kurt) |>
  flextable::flextable()
```


## 4.5.6 Summary of Diagnostic Findings

```{r diag-summary}
diagnostic_summary <- tibble(
  Issue = c("Multicollinearity",
            "Heteroskedasticity",
            "Autocorrelation",
            "Outliers / influential months",
            "Normality of residuals",
            "Functional form"),
  Evidence = c(
    sprintf("Max VIF = %.2f; max |correlation| = %.2f",
            max(vif_results$VIF), max(abs(correlation_pairs$Correlation))),
    sprintf("Breusch-Pagan p = %.3f; White p = %.3f",
            bp_test$p.value, white_test$p.value),
    sprintf("DW = %.2f; BG(1) p = %.3f; BG(12) p = %.3f",
            dw_test$statistic, bg_test_1$p.value, bg_test_12$p.value),
    sprintf("%d months above Cook's 4/n; %d high-leverage months",
            sum(influence_table$Influential), sum(influence_table$High_Leverage)),
    sprintf("Shapiro-Wilk p = %.3f; Jarque-Bera p = %.3f",
            shapiro_result$p.value, jb_p),
    sprintf("RESET p = %.3f", reset_result$p.value)
  ),
  Problem_Detected = c(
    if_else(max(vif_results$VIF) > 5, "Yes", "No"),
    if_else(min(bp_test$p.value, white_test$p.value) < inference_alpha, "Yes", "No"),
    if_else(min(dw_test$p.value, bg_test_1$p.value, bg_test_12$p.value) < inference_alpha, "Yes", "No"),
    if_else(sum(influence_table$Influential) > 0, "Yes", "No"),
    if_else(min(shapiro_result$p.value, jb_p) < inference_alpha, "Yes", "No"),
    if_else(reset_result$p.value < inference_alpha, "Yes", "No")
  )
)

diagnostic_summary |>
  flextable::flextable()
```

















# 4.6 Model Improvement

This section responds to the problems found in 4.5. Each remedy is applied only where the diagnostics or the data justify it, and the improved model is then compared with the baseline.


## 4.6.1 Problems Addressed and Remedies

```{r improve-plan}
tibble(
  Problem = c(
    "Extreme manufacturing growth values (base effects from the 2020 lockdowns)",
    "Influential crisis months (Cook's distance above 4/n)",
    "Standard errors may be affected by heteroskedasticity or autocorrelation the tests could not detect"
  ),
  Remedy = c(
    "Winsorize manufacturing growth at its 5th and 95th percentiles",
    "Keep the months in the model; refit without them as a sensitivity check",
    "Report Newey-West (HAC) robust standard errors"
  ),
  Why = c(
    sprintf("Readings as high as %+.0f%% reflect a collapsed 2020 base, not real expansion, and raise the leverage of the 2021 months that carry them",
            max(model_data$manafactuting_prod_growth)),
    "They are real market events (e.g., COVID-19, 2022 rate hikes); deleting them would hide risk an investor actually faces",
    "HAC standard errors stay valid whether or not these problems are present, so inference does not depend on the tests having enough power with 96 months"
  )
) |>
  flextable::flextable()
```


## 4.6.2 Remedy 1: Winsorizing Manufacturing Growth

Winsorizing replaces values below the 5th percentile with the 5th percentile, and values above the 95th percentile with the 95th percentile. The month stays in the sample; only its extreme value is capped.

```{r improve-winsorize}
manufacturing_limits <- quantile(
  model_data$manafactuting_prod_growth,
  probs = c(0.05, 0.95)
)

improved_data <- model_data |>
  mutate(
    manafactuting_prod_growth = pmin(
      pmax(manafactuting_prod_growth, manufacturing_limits[1]),
      manufacturing_limits[2]
    )
  )

tibble(
  Statistic = c("5th percentile cap", "95th percentile cap",
                "Months capped", "Original min", "Original max",
                "Winsorized min", "Winsorized max"),
  Value = c(manufacturing_limits[1], manufacturing_limits[2],
            sum(model_data$manafactuting_prod_growth != improved_data$manafactuting_prod_growth),
            min(model_data$manafactuting_prod_growth), max(model_data$manafactuting_prod_growth),
            min(improved_data$manafactuting_prod_growth), max(improved_data$manafactuting_prod_growth))
) |>
  flextable::flextable()

improved_lm <- lm(reformulate(".", response = dep_var), data = improved_data)
```

The table below shows how capping changes the leverage of the months whose manufacturing value was capped.

```{r improve-winsorize-leverage}
tibble(
  Month = format(diag_months),
  Original_Value = model_data$manafactuting_prod_growth,
  Winsorized_Value = improved_data$manafactuting_prod_growth,
  Leverage_Before = hatvalues(baseline_lm),
  Leverage_After = hatvalues(improved_lm)
) |>
  filter(Original_Value != Winsorized_Value) |>
  mutate(Above_Cutoff_After = Leverage_After > leverage_cutoff) |>
  flextable::flextable()
```


## 4.6.3 Remedy 2: Newey-West (HAC) Robust Standard Errors

Newey-West standard errors adjust for both heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation (HAC). They do not change the coefficient estimates, only their standard errors, t-statistics and p-values. The number of lags follows the common rule of thumb floor(4(n/100)^(2/9)).

```{r improve-hac}
hac_lag <- floor(4 * (nobs(improved_lm) / 100)^(2 / 9))

improved_vcov <- sandwich::NeweyWest(
  improved_lm,
  lag = hac_lag,
  prewhite = FALSE,
  adjust = TRUE
)

improved_results <- lmtest::coeftest(improved_lm, vcov. = improved_vcov) |>
  broom::tidy() |>
  left_join(
    lmtest::coefci(improved_lm, vcov. = improved_vcov, level = 1 - inference_alpha) |>
      as.data.frame() |>
      rownames_to_column("term") |>
      setNames(c("term", "conf.low", "conf.high")),
    by = "term"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Decision = if_else(
      p.value < inference_alpha,
      "Reject H0; evidence of a linear association",
      "Fail to reject H0; insufficient evidence"
    )
  )

tibble(Setting = "Newey-West lags", Value = hac_lag) |>
  flextable::flextable()

improved_results |>
  mutate(p.value = format.pval(p.value, digits = 3, eps = 0.0001)) |>
  flextable::flextable()
```

```{r improve-hac-joint}
# Joint test: do the eight non-PSEi factors add information, using HAC standard errors?
improved_market_lm <- lm(BDO_return ~ PSEI_return, data = improved_data)

hac_joint_test <- lmtest::waldtest(
  improved_market_lm,
  improved_lm,
  vcov = improved_vcov,
  test = "F"
)

tibble(
  Test = "Eight non-PSEi factors jointly zero (HAC)",
  F_Statistic = hac_joint_test$F[2],
  Numerator_DF = abs(hac_joint_test$Df[2]),
  p.value = hac_joint_test$`Pr(>F)`[2]
) |>
  mutate(
    Decision = if_else(
      p.value < inference_alpha,
      "Reject H0; the group adds explanatory information",
      "Fail to reject H0; insufficient evidence the group adds information"
    ),
    p.value = format.pval(p.value, digits = 3, eps = 0.0001)
  ) |>
  flextable::flextable()
```


## 4.6.4 Remedy 3: Sensitivity to Influential Months

The improved model is refit without the months flagged by Cook's distance in 4.5.4. If the main conclusions hold without them, the results do not depend on a few unusual months.

```{r improve-sensitivity}
influential_months <- influence_table |>
  filter(Influential) |>
  pull(Month)

sensitivity_lm <- lm(
  reformulate(".", response = dep_var),
  data = improved_data[!influence_table$Influential, ]
)

tibble(Months_Removed = paste(influential_months, collapse = ", "),
       Observations_Left = nobs(sensitivity_lm)) |>
  flextable::flextable()
```


## 4.6.5 Baseline vs. Improved Model

The table compares each coefficient across three versions:

- **Baseline:** Original model with ordinary (OLS) standard errors, as in 4.3.
- **Improved:** Winsorized manufacturing growth with Newey-West standard errors.
- **Without influential months:** Improved specification refit without the Cook's distance months, with Newey-West standard errors.

```{r improve-comparison}
tidy_with_vcov <- function(fit, vcov_matrix, label) {
  lmtest::coeftest(fit, vcov. = vcov_matrix) |>
    broom::tidy() |>
    transmute(
      term,
      !!paste0(label, "_Estimate") := estimate,
      !!paste0(label, "_SE")       := std.error,
      !!paste0(label, "_p")        := p.value
    )
}

sensitivity_vcov <- sandwich::NeweyWest(
  sensitivity_lm, lag = hac_lag, prewhite = FALSE, adjust = TRUE
)

coefficient_comparison <- tidy_with_vcov(baseline_lm, vcov(baseline_lm), "Baseline") |>
  left_join(tidy_with_vcov(improved_lm, improved_vcov, "Improved"), by = "term") |>
  left_join(tidy_with_vcov(sensitivity_lm, sensitivity_vcov, "NoInfluential"), by = "term") |>
  mutate(
    Same_Sign = sign(Baseline_Estimate) == sign(Improved_Estimate) &
                sign(Improved_Estimate) == sign(NoInfluential_Estimate),
    Same_5pct_Decision = (Baseline_p < inference_alpha) == (Improved_p < inference_alpha) &
                         (Improved_p < inference_alpha) == (NoInfluential_p < inference_alpha)
  )

coefficient_comparison |>
  mutate(across(ends_with("_p"), ~ format.pval(.x, digits = 3, eps = 0.0001))) |>
  flextable::flextable()
```

```{r improve-fit-comparison}
fit_summary <- function(fit, label) {
  tibble(
    Model = label,
    N = nobs(fit),
    R_Squared = summary(fit)$r.squared,
    Adjusted_R_Squared = summary(fit)$adj.r.squared,
    AIC = AIC(fit),
    BIC = BIC(fit),
    Max_Leverage = max(hatvalues(fit)),
    Breusch_Pagan_p = lmtest::bptest(fit)$p.value,
    Breusch_Godfrey_12_p = lmtest::bgtest(fit, order = 12)$p.value
  )
}

bind_rows(
  fit_summary(baseline_lm, "Baseline"),
  fit_summary(improved_lm, "Improved"),
  fit_summary(sensitivity_lm, "Without influential months")
) |>
  flextable::flextable()
```

AIC and BIC for the model without influential months are not comparable with the other two, because it uses fewer observations. R-squared and fit measures are reported for completeness; the improved model is not chosen for a higher R-squared but because its inference is more reliable.

```{r improve-coef-plot, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5}
# Coefficients with 95% confidence intervals: baseline (OLS) vs. improved (HAC)
bind_rows(
  broom::tidy(baseline_lm, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 1 - inference_alpha) |>
    mutate(Model = "Baseline (OLS SE)"),
  improved_results |>
    mutate(Model = "Improved (HAC SE)")
) |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  group_by(term) |>
  mutate(scale = max(abs(c(conf.low, conf.high)))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(across(c(estimate, conf.low, conf.high), ~ .x / scale)) |>
  ggplot(aes(estimate, term, shape = Model)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  labs(title = "Coefficient estimates and 95% confidence intervals",
       subtitle = "Each factor rescaled by its largest interval bound so all fit on one axis",
       x = "Scaled estimate", y = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r improve-summary}
tibble(
  Check = c(
    "Coefficients that keep the same sign across all three versions",
    "Coefficients with the same 5% decision across all three versions",
    "Factors significant at 5% in the improved model (HAC)"
  ),
  Result = c(
    sprintf("%d of %d", sum(coefficient_comparison$Same_Sign), nrow(coefficient_comparison)),
    sprintf("%d of %d", sum(coefficient_comparison$Same_5pct_Decision), nrow(coefficient_comparison)),
    improved_results |>
      filter(term != "(Intercept)", p.value < inference_alpha) |>
      pull(term) |>
      paste(collapse = ", ")
  )
) |>
  flextable::flextable()
```
